title: Online Single-Item (Posted-Price) Auction
body_html:
Online Single-Item (Posted-Price) Auction

The online single-item auction sells one indivisible good to bidders who arrive one at a time. While the item is unsold, the auctioneer posts a take-it-or-leave-it price that may depend only on the bids already seen; the current bidder either accepts (and the auction ends) or departs forever.

Model

Each bidder is presented as a pair $(b, v)$: an identity $b$ drawn from an identity set $\mathcal{B}$ and a (real-valued) value $v$. The auction is determined by a single ingredient — a threshold rule that maps the history of previously rejected bids to either

  • no acceptable price (the auction refuses to sell to the next bidder), or
  • a pair $(p, b^\star)$ giving a price $p$ and an identity tag $b^\star$.

A bidder $(b, v)$ arriving against threshold $(p, b^\star)$ is admitted precisely when

$$ p < v \quad\text{or}\quad (p = v \;\text{and}\; b^\star \le b). $$

That is: clearing the price strictly is enough; at exactly the price, the bidder additionally needs an identity that meets the threshold's identity tag. The identity tag is what lets the rule tell apart two bidders sitting at the same price, without ever appealing to an external tie-breaking oracle.

The first admitted bidder wins the item at the threshold price $p$ and the auction ends; every later arrival sees the auction already closed and departs with no allocation and no payment.

Welfare and utility

Fix $n$ bidders presented in arrival order as a profile $f$. The social welfare $A.\mathrm{welfare}(f)$ is the value of whichever bidder is admitted, or $0$ if every bidder is rejected. The bidder-$i$ utility $A.\mathrm{utility}(f, v, i)$ is the quasi-linear payoff $v_i - p$ when bidder $i$ is admitted at price $p$, and $0$ otherwise.

Remarks

Why an identity tag on the threshold?

A first attempt at the model would post only a price $p$, with no identity tag, and resolve "price equals value" however convenient. Two natural choices both fail the random-order competitive guarantee (Sample-Then-Threshold Rule Is 1/4-Competitive):

  • Strict comparison ($p < v$) rejects every bidder whose value exactly matches the threshold. With two bidders of equal value $M$, the observe phase records $M$, the strict test rejects the second bidder, and welfare is $0$ on every permutation (Strict Value Comparison Breaks the Competitive Guarantee).
  • Weak comparison ($p \le v$) admits any later bidder whose value matches the threshold. On the needle profile $v = (M, 0, \ldots, 0)$, the observe phase records $0$, and the test $0 \le 0$ admits the first phase-2 arrival regardless of value; expected welfare is only $M/n$ (Weak Value Comparison Degrades to 1/n on the Needle Profile).

The identity tag fixes both failures. At the threshold price, the admit-or-reject decision additionally consults the bidder's identity against the tag, so the sample-then-threshold rule can specify which tied bidder to admit. This pushes tie-breaking into the auction itself rather than into an external mechanism or a hidden value-distinctness assumption, and the resulting analysis only needs identities to be distinct — not values.

Format-independent truthfulness

Because the price posted to bidder $i$ depends only on the first $i - 1$ bids, no bidder can move their own price. Truthful bidding is therefore dominant for every threshold rule of this shape, not just a particular pricing strategy (Truthful Bidding Is Dominant in the Online Auction).

Position in the library

Concrete threshold rules yield the three results:

  • Truthfulness — every history-dependent rule is DSIC (Truthful Bidding Is Dominant in the Online Auction).
  • Deterministic impossibility — worst-case arrival order admits no constant competitive ratio (No Deterministic Constant Competitive Ratio).
  • Random-order guarantee — under a uniformly random arrival order, the sample-then-threshold rule achieves a constant ($1/4$) competitive ratio (Sample-Then-Threshold Rule Is 1/4-Competitive).

Lean formalization

In EconCSLib, an auction is the type SingleItemAuction B F, parameterised by an identity type B and a numeric type F (any linearly ordered field). It has a single field threshold : List (B × F) → WithTop (Lex (F × B)). The codomain encodes the two cases of the model directly:

  • ⊤ : WithTop (Lex (F × B)) is the "no acceptable price" sentinel.
  • ↑(toLex (p, b⋆)) : WithTop (Lex (F × B)) is the finite threshold with price $p$ and identity tag $b^\star$, lexicographic on the price first and the identity second.

The acceptance test is the single inequality threshold h ≤ ↑(toLex (v_i, b_i)) in WithTop (Lex (F × B)). Unfolding via Prod.Lex.le_iff gives exactly the disjunction $p < v_i \lor (p = v_i \land b^\star \le b_i)$ from the model.

A run of the auction plugs SingleItemAuction into the generic online-algorithm framework Online.OnlineAlgorithm Input State Output, whose single field step : State → Option Input → State × Option Output consumes one input and emits the next state plus an optional output. The auction state

$$ \mathrm{AuctionState}\,B\,F \;=\; \mathsf{unsold}\,(\text{history} : \mathrm{List}\,(B \times F)) \;\mid\; \mathsf{sold}\,(\text{winner} : \mathbb{N})\,(\text{price} : F) $$

carries in the unsold case the list of previously rejected $(identity, value)$ pairs — the only thing the threshold rule is allowed to read. The embedding A.online reads:

step | .unsold h, some (bi, vi) => match A.threshold h with | ⊤ => (.unsold (h ++ [(bi, vi)]), none) | ↑t => if t ≤ toLex (vi, bi) then (.sold h.length (ofLex t).1, some (ofLex t).1) else (.unsold (h ++ [(bi, vi)]), none) | .unsold h, none => (.unsold h, none) | .sold w p, _ => (.sold w p, none)

A.welfare and A.utility are defined for n-bidder profiles indexed by Fin n. A.welfare f is given by the recursive helper welfareAux, which threads the rejection history through the trajectory so that small concrete profiles reduce cleanly under simp. A.utility f v i factors through stateBeforeStep f i, the auction state reached before bidder $i$ is processed; this lemma isolates bidder $i$'s local view from the global trajectory and is the structural ingredient of the DSIC proof (Truthful Bidding Is Dominant in the Online Auction).

Two-type-parameter design

Keeping the identity type B separate from the value type F enables identity-aware pricing (needed for the sample-then-threshold analysis) while leaving the core auction theory generic. Two indexing conventions coexist: List (B × F) is natural for the streaming input, while Fin n → B × F is natural for the game-theoretic layer (fixed agents, single-bidder deviations via Function.update, random arrival via Equiv.Perm (Fin n)). The two are bridged by List.ofFn.

The sample-then-threshold auction (Sample-Then-Threshold Rule Is 1/4-Competitive) takes Function.Injective g (identity injectivity) as its hypothesis, rather than the mathematically unnatural Function.Injective v (value injectivity) that would be needed without an identity tag.

References

  • [Roughgarden 2016, Lecture 2, Problem 2.1] Tim Roughgarden, Twenty Lectures on Algorithmic Game Theory, Cambridge University Press. Online posted-price single-item auction and its analysis.
  • [AGT, Chapter 1, Section 1.3.2] Nisan, Roughgarden, Tardos, and Vazirani, Algorithmic Game Theory. Sealed-bid single-item auctions as the basic algorithmic game theory example.
